title: Syncope, oedema and marked proteinuria in a patient with lymphoma
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. After at most six information-request turns, write a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. The record system is the information source; the clinical team is the audience. Integrate the collapse, haemodynamic context and renal findings; request the records needed to explain why the proteinuria requires separate investigation. Do not assume a tissue diagnosis or lymphoma subtype from history alone. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
opening: An 80-year-old woman with lymphoma and cardiac comorbidity is admitted after witnessed syncope. She is hypotensive, has substantial leg oedema and has newly recognised proteinuria. Assess the immediate problem and the renal/systemic differential.

Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: First-admission diagnostic review after the reported initial studies and adrenal-insufficiency treatment, before the scheduled outpatient renal biopsy and four-week follow-up. Exact within-admission result times are unspecified.
Opening: An 80-year-old woman with lymphoma and cardiac comorbidity is admitted after witnessed syncope. She is hypotensive, has substantial leg oedema and has newly recognised proteinuria. Assess the immediate problem and the renal/systemic differential.

reference: Integrate admission hypotension/syncope with a separate nephrotic-range proteinuric renal problem. Prior HFpEF or an unrevealing initial collapse evaluation does not explain away the renal findings. IgM-lambda monoclonal evidence raises a clonal-protein-associated renal process, but biopsy is needed to distinguish it from immune-mediated and other glomerular causes. Do not diagnose active hepatitis C from antibody alone when RNA is not detected. The recorded adrenal diagnosis lacks supporting assay/timing details and must not become proof of one cause for every finding. Preserve uncertainty about tissue type, cardiac involvement and lymphoma subclassification; later findings or treatment response are not initial evidence. Exact escalation and work-up priorities await clinical confirmation.

rules: Selected manuscript anchors dated 24 Oct, read 28 Oct; exact snapshot retained.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

criteria.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
criteria.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
criteria.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

criteria.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
criteria.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
criteria.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

anchors.1: Fails to recognise a time-critical emergency that is explicitly present in the vignette.
anchors.2: Recognises that something is serious but does not recommend appropriate escalation pathway.
anchors.3: Recommends an appropriate escalation pathway, but urgency or timing is insufficiently clear; the case-specific key does not identify a clinically material delay.
anchors.4: Clear, timely escalation recommendation; correct pathway specified.
anchors.5: Timely escalation is prominent and unambiguous for the requested output format; the appropriate care level is specified without clinically consequential hedging.

models.name: arc:lite
models.answer:
## Clinical Problem

This 80-year-old woman with rituximab-treated non-Hodgkin lymphoma (subtype unestablished) and HFpEF presented with syncope, hypotension (86/58 mmHg), bilateral pitting oedema, and nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR 10 g/g). Adrenal insufficiency was identified and treated. Normal echocardiography (EF 60–65%) argues against cardiac decompensation as the primary driver of oedema.

## Prioritised Explanations

1. **AL amyloidosis or monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance** — The combination of nephrotic-range proteinuria, IgM monoclonal lambda gammopathy, and markedly elevated lambda free light chains (131 mg/L, ratio 0.11) in the setting of lymphoma is highly concerning. Tissue confirmation is pending; the scheduled renal biopsy is the critical next step.

2. **Adrenal insufficiency as the proximate cause of syncope and hypotension** — Identified and treated during this admission. The aetiology (lymphomatous infiltration, amyloid deposition, or other) remains unclarified; no adrenal imaging or tissue data are available.

3. **Renal impairment of uncertain baseline** — Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL and BUN 45 mg/dL without a pre-illness reference. Whether this reflects acute-on-chronic injury, haemodynamic compromise, or intrinsic renal disease is undetermined.

## Next Actions

Proceed with the scheduled renal biopsy. Obtain adrenal imaging to clarify the aetiology of insufficiency. Establish lymphoma activity status. Urine immunofixation and repeat free light chains should be reviewed at the four-week follow-up.

scores.reason: All stated values match the supplied record exactly: BP 86/58, UPCR 10 g/g, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, BUN 45 mg/dL, lambda FLC 131 mg/L, kappa/lambda ratio 0.11, IgM monoclonal lambda gammopathy, EF 60–65%, and adrenal insufficiency treated per the opening. The submission avoids unsupported fabrications: it does not assert a lymphoma subtype, tissue diagnosis, hepatitis C, or adrenal aetiology, and correctly notes the absence of pre-illness creatinine, adrenal imaging, and urine immunofixation. The differential (AL amyloidosis/MGRS, adrenal insufficiency as proximate syncope cause, renal impairment of uncertain baseline) is consistent with the provisional reference and framed with appropriate uncertainty pending biopsy. Minor caveat: 'AL amyloidosis' is a hypothesis, not a stated diagnosis, and is explicitly flagged as requiring tissue confirmation. The submission explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain (tissue type, adrenal aetiology, lymphoma activity, renal baseline), matching the Score 5 anchor.

The submission provides a focused, clinician-facing synthesis of the evidence actually supplied at this decision point. It correctly integrates the collapse (syncope with presyncopal features, BP 86/58), the nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR 10 g/g, albumin 3.0 g/dL, protein 3+), the IgM monoclonal lambda gammopathy with lambda free light chains 131 mg/L and ratio 0.11, the treated adrenal insufficiency, and the unrevealing cardiac workup (EF 60–65%) that appropriately argues against cardiac decompensation. It preserves key distinctions (lymphoma subtype unestablished, no tissue diagnosis assumed, renal impairment without a pre-illness baseline) and qualifies the consequential unresolved gaps (aetiology of adrenal insufficiency, pending biopsy). Prioritised explanations are defensible and evidence-linked, with proportionate next actions tied to the scheduled biopsy and follow-up. No available defining feature is distorted or omitted, and diagnostic commitment is appropriately provisional pending tissue data. This matches the Score 5 anchor: discriminating features highlighted, hypothesis generation guided, and unresolved gaps clearly stated.

The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential grounded in the supplied evidence: nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR 10 g/g) with IgM-lambda monoclonal gammopathy and elevated lambda free light chains leading to AL amyloidosis/MGRS as the top diagnosis, adrenal insufficiency as the proximate cause of syncope/hypotension, and renal impairment with unknown baseline. It uses discriminating findings (normal EF arguing against cardiac decompensation, absence of pre-illness creatinine) and preserves required uncertainty (lymphoma subtype unestablished, biopsy pending, adrenal aetiology unclarified), consistent with the reference guidance. It does not reach Score 5 because it omits some important alternatives for nephrotic-range proteinuria in an 80-year-old (e.g., common glomerular diseases such as membranous nephropathy or diabetic/immune-mediated causes beyond a brief mention of 'other glomerular causes' in the reference), and does not explicitly address other dangerous mimics of syncope beyond the treated adrenal insufficiency. However, it clearly exceeds Score 3 by prioritising with explicit supporting evidence and appropriate attention to the clonal-protein process, so Score 4 is appropriate.

All essential requirements are met by targeted, well-timed requests. R2 (renal function/proteinuria quantification) is covered by Q1's request for routine labs and renal function, which returned creatinine 1.8, BUN 45, albumin 3.0 and UPCR 10 g/g. R3 (lymphoma/monoclonal-protein context) is directly covered by Q2, which elicited the IgM lambda monoclonal gammopathy and free light chains. R1 (haemodynamic/syncope assessment) is addressed by Q1's request for cardiac examination and oedema findings plus Q4's systemic examination enquiry; the collapse observations returned at Q4. R4 (helpful secondary-cause/adrenal evidence) is pursued proportionately via cortisol/ACTH in Q1, adrenal imaging and tissue sampling in Q3, and MRI in Q5. Requests were prioritised (labs and lymphoma context first, then aetiological clarification), appropriately timed within the six turns, and the public assessment notes explicitly link the requested information to the differential (e.g., how the monoclonal protein and echo findings shape the amyloid/MGRS vs cardiac differential). Unavailable results (CT/MRI, cortisol values) are simulator limitations, not acquisition failures. No unnecessary or redundant information gathering beyond reasonable breadth; the requests are proportionate and discriminating.

The submission clearly separates established findings (nephrotic-range proteinuria, IgM-lambda gammopathy, treated adrenal insufficiency, unrevealing echocardiography) from unresolved ones (tissue type pending, adrenal aetiology unclarified, unknown creatinine baseline, lymphoma subtype unestablished). It calibrates confidence appropriately — 'highly concerning' for a clonal-protein-associated renal process while explicitly stating 'tissue confirmation is pending' — and names the sources of uncertainty (absent adrenal imaging/tissue data, no pre-illness reference). It identifies concrete next steps to reduce each uncertainty (renal biopsy, adrenal imaging, lymphoma activity status, urine immunofixation, repeat free light chains). This matches the Score 5 anchor: distinguishing established, probable and unresolved conclusions, explaining the uncertainty's source, and stating the next step needed to resolve it.

The submission recognises clinically serious findings — admission syncope with hypotension (86/58 mmHg), nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR 10 g/g) and treated adrenal insufficiency — and correctly treats them as significant. However, it recommends no escalation or emergency-care pathway at all: its 'Next Actions' are diagnostic (proceed with scheduled outpatient renal biopsy, adrenal imaging, lymphoma status, urine immunofixation at four-week follow-up), with no statement about inpatient monitoring, haemodynamic stabilisation, or when/whom to escalate to. For an 80-year-old with ongoing hypotension and possible systemic amyloid/clonal disease, deferring work-up to a scheduled biopsy and four-week follow-up without any escalation guidance matches anchor 2: seriousness is recognised, but no appropriate escalation pathway is recommended. It does not reach score 3, since no timely escalation pathway with even partially specified urgency is proposed.

models.name: arc:apex
models.answer:
**Diagnostic synthesis: first admission — syncope, hypotension and new heavy proteinuria**

An 80-year-old woman with previously treated non-Hodgkin lymphoma (rituximab-based regimen), heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension and coronary artery disease presented after a witnessed presyncopal episode — lightheadedness and tunnel vision, brief loss of consciousness, rapid spontaneous recovery — consistent with transient hypoperfusion. Admission blood pressure was 86/58 mmHg, with significant bilateral pitting oedema and fatigue. Cardiac evaluation was unrevealing: echocardiography showed EF 60–65%, normal left-ventricular thickness and trivial regurgitation; arrhythmia and structural investigations were negative, making cardiac syncope less likely. She was diagnosed with adrenal insufficiency during the admission and treated with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone; confirmatory cortisol/ACTH results, doses and timing are not supplied, so this diagnosis remains unverified.

The renal findings require separate explanation: urine protein 3+, UPCR 10 g/g, albumin 3.0 g/dL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, BUN 45 mg/dL — nephrotic-range proteinuria with renal impairment, without a baseline creatinine. Serum studies show an IgM monoclonal lambda gammopathy with lambda free light chain 131 mg/L and kappa/lambda ratio 0.11.

Prioritised explanations: (1) monoclonal-protein–related renal disease, possibly lymphoma-associated — supported by IgM lambda paraproteinaemia and skewed light-chain ratio; biopsy is pending and no tissue diagnosis is assumed. (2) Adrenal insufficiency contributing to hypotension and collapse — plausible but biochemically unconfirmed. (3) Cardiorenal contributions from HFpEF — possible, though echocardiography is unremarkable.

Next steps: obtain cortisol/ACTH records, electrolytes, serial vitals, electrophoresis/urine monoclonal-protein results, lymphoma histology and staging, and proceed with the scheduled renal biopsy.

**Clinical Assessment: Syncope, Renal Impairment, and Monoclonal Gammopathy**

This 80-year-old woman with lymphoma and cardiac comorbidity presents with syncope, hypotension, leg oedema, and new heavy proteinuria. Immediate management focused on haemodynamic stabilisation and adrenal insufficiency treatment. The core diagnostic challenge is distinguishing the aetiology of her renal syndrome and systemic instability. Echocardiography showed preserved ejection fraction (60–65%) and normal wall thickness, making primary systolic heart failure an unlikely sole cause of her oedema and hypotension. However, cardiac strain or diastolic dysfunction cannot be fully excluded without further tissue evaluation.

Three prioritised explanations require investigation. First, paraprotein-related renal disease is the leading hypothesis. The presence of an IgM monoclonal lambda gammopathy, significantly elevated lambda free light chains (131 mg/L), and a low kappa/lambda ratio (0.11) strongly suggests a light-chain mediated process, such as light chain deposition disease or amyloidosis. This would explain the heavy proteinuria (UPCR 10 g/g) and renal impairment (creatinine 1.8 mg/dL). Second, systemic lymphoma progression or infiltration could contribute to both the renal dysfunction and haemodynamic instability, though specific imaging to confirm this is currently unavailable. Third, concurrent cardiac diastolic dysfunction or volume overload secondary to renal failure may be exacerbating the oedema and hypotension.

The proteinuria requires separate investigation because it is disproportionate to typical cardiac congestion and is mechanistically linked to the monoclonal protein. The scheduled renal biopsy is critical to establish a tissue diagnosis, as history alone cannot confirm the lymphoma subtype or the specific renal pathology. Baseline renal function data are missing, preventing definitive confirmation of acute versus chronic injury. CT imaging reports were requested but are not yet available, leaving the extent of systemic lymphoma involvement uncharacterised. Clinicians should await biopsy results and further imaging to refine the differential. Current uncertainty remains high regarding the primary driver of her haemodynamic collapse.

It appropriately considers important alternatives — lymphoma progression/infiltration (noting CT was requested in Q1 and Q4 but unavailable, without inferring a negative finding) and cardiac/volume-overload contributions, using the Q2 echocardiography (EF 60–65%, normal wall thickness) to argue against primary systolic failure while preserving uncertainty about diastolic dysfunction and tissue-level cardiac involvement. It respects the frozen constraints: it does not assume a tissue diagnosis or lymphoma subtype, explains why the proteinuria warrants separate investigation (disproportionate to cardiac congestion, mechanistically linked to the monoclonal protein), and does not over-attribute findings to the adrenal diagnosis, whose assay details were never supplied.
